metadata.title: Measuring process quality in early childhood education and care through Situational Judgement Questions (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS Starting Strong 2018 Field Trial data from early childhood education and care (ECEC) staff in two target populations (centres for children under age 3 and centres at ISCED Level 02). The field trial implemented a rotated questionnaire design and required minimum sample sizes per country (minimum 30 centres and 240 staff per country) to support the survey design and planned analyses. The paper does not report the use of complex survey weights or any specific weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) in the provided text, so weighting strategy cannot be confirmed from the excerpt. For Main Survey implementation, analysts should follow TALIS Starting Strong survey documentation for complex sampling (stratification/clustering) and apply the recommended weights when estimating country-level comparisons and psychometric parameters.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This OECD report evaluates the reliability, validity, and measurement invariance of Situational Judgement Questions (SJQs) using IRT-based nominal response modelling and factor-score estimates, rather than producing cognitive achievement scores with plausible values (PVs). Because the dependent variables are SJQ response patterns and derived factor scores for process-quality constructs (not PV-based achievement outcomes), PV handling is not applicable. The excerpt also does not describe a missing-data strategy (e.g., deletion or imputation), so missing-data handling is not reported in the provided text.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analyses are based on TALIS Starting Strong 2018 Field Trial data. The field trial included two target populations: (1) staff working in centres for children under age 3 and (2) staff working in centres belonging to ISCED Level 02. A rotated questionnaire design was used due to the large number of field trial questions, with a minimum sample size requirement of 30 centres per country and 240 ECEC staff members per country. The paper also reports that SJQs were scored for both target populations by experts (QEG/TAG/NPMs and ECEC experts), and that measurement invariance across the two target populations was assessed using the nominal response modelling (NRM) approach; however, no additional student-level inclusion/exclusion rules (e.g., missing response thresholds) are specified in the provided excerpt.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report evaluates the psychometric properties of Situational Judgement Questions (SJQs) designed to measure early childhood education and care (ECEC) process quality in the TALIS Starting Strong 2018 Field Trial. The study compares two SJQ response formats (Likert-scale vs forced choice) and multiple scoring approaches, including ranking, popularity-based scoring, and Nominal Response Modelling (NRM) within an IRT framework. Reliability is assessed via internal consistency and empirical reliability, and validity is examined through construct/criterion validity using correlations with related questionnaire items and staff background measures (notably staff self-efficacy and formal education). Measurement invariance is tested across two target populations (under-3 centres vs ISCED Level 02 centres), with scalar invariance largely met for Likert formats (except SJQ29 showing metric invariance), while forced-choice formats show poorer invariance. The report recommends using Likert-format SJQs and NRM scoring for the Main Survey, while noting limitations including small field-trial sample sizes that prevent invariance testing across countries and the absence of direct observation to rule out social desirability.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD technical report focused on instrument development and psychometric evaluation (reliability, validity, and measurement invariance) rather than predictive modelling. Consequently, there are no ML algorithms to extract, no PV-based achievement outcomes, and no structured predictive findings to tabulate. The excerpt also does not provide author names or the full list of participating countries (countries are explicitly anonymised in Table 2.1), so country-level ISO codes and per-country student counts cannot be reliably reconstructed from the provided text.
